strengths: Addresses a clearly under-explored problem: embedding models today only accept textual instructions, and the paper proposes a principled way to inject visual prompts (points/boxes/masks) via a pretrained segmentation model (SAM2) combined with a VLM, producing joint entity-level and global embeddings.

Introduces SCaR, a large-scale (1M sample) Segmentation-and-Scene Caption Retrieval benchmark built from five public datasets, with a carefully designed negative-generation pipeline (global-context/relation/object swaps) and a multi-stage LLM-then-human filtering process to ensure quality; this fills a genuine gap since no prior benchmark evaluates visual-interactive image-to-text retrieval with hard, semantically informed negatives.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements: VIRTUE outperforms numerous CLIP-based and VLM-based baselines (GME, LamRA, VLM2Vec, MMRet, UniME) on 36 MMEB tasks (3.1%-8.5% gains) and 5 SCaR tasks (15.2%-20.3% gains), covering both in-domain and out-of-domain settings.

Extensive ablation and hyperparameter studies (VLM backbone choice, instruction presence, image resolution, segmentation-streamline alternatives such as cropping/Prompter, SAM2 model size, MLP depth, segmentation embedding length, LoRA rank, batch size, sampling points) that support many of the design decisions.

Useful qualitative case studies demonstrating practical utility of visual prompting, such as on-the-fly correction of VQA/retrieval errors and interactive image-to-image retrieval, illustrating real application value beyond benchmark numbers.
Reasonably transparent reproducibility and ethics statements, with partial benchmark and code released, and clear documentation of data collection prompts and filtering criteria in the appendix.
weaknesses: The benchmark's ground-truth captions and negative distractors are generated by GPT-4V rather than fully human-authored; while an LLM-then-human filtering pipeline is applied to the evaluation set, the much larger training set is only 'indirectly' assessed by downstream model performance, leaving open the possibility of systematic GPT-4V biases or artifacts propagating through training data.

Comparisons on SCaR for visual-interactive capability may be somewhat unfair to baselines: none of the compared embedding models natively support bounding-box inputs, so they are given a textualized bbox string, which is not their designed interaction modality; this makes it harder to disentangle gains due to the proposed segmentation-embedding architecture versus simply having access to explicit spatial input in a format the baseline wasn't designed for.

The core technical contribution is a relatively straightforward integration of an off-the-shelf SAM2 segmentation model with an existing VLM embedding pipeline (via a small conv+MLP connector and LoRA-based contrastive finetuning); the architectural novelty is incremental relative to prior VLM-embedder work (e.g., VLM2Vec, GME), and the paper's main differentiator is largely the new benchmark rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique.

Quantitative evaluation of the interactive image-to-image (I2I) retrieval capability -- one of the two visual-interactive scenarios motivated in the introduction (Fig. 1) -- is not performed; only a small qualitative case study is presented in the appendix, explicitly citing copyright/ethical constraints, which weakens the evidence for this claimed capability.

The added computational/latency overhead of running a full SAM2 segmentation backbone alongside the VLM (image encoder, prompt encoder, mask decoder) is not analyzed or discussed, which is relevant for the practicality of the proposed universal embedder in real deployment.

Experiments are limited to a single VLM family (Qwen2-VL 2B/7B) as backbone; it is unclear whether the reported gains generalize to other VLM architectures or scales, limiting the demonstrated generality of the approach.

Some improvements attributed to VIRTUE are partly confounded by additional finetuning steps on SCaR-train; although the paper does apply +SCaR-train to baselines for fairness, the larger baseline degradation (e.g., catastrophic forgetting in VLM2Vec/MMRet) suggests the comparison may be sensitive to training-schedule choices rather than purely architectural advantages.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: enabling embedding models to consume visual prompts (points/boxes/masks) in addition to text, which could meaningfully extend applicability of VLM-based retrievers to localized, user-specified regions.

Introduces a large-scale (1M sample) benchmark, SCaR, built from five diverse public datasets (RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, VisualGenome, COCO-Stuff, ADE20K) with a non-trivial negative-generation scheme (global-context, relation, and object swaps) and a multi-stage LLM+human filtering pipeline, which is a useful community resource if released.

Strong quantitative results: VIRTUE reports consistent improvements over a wide range of CLIP- and VLM-based baselines across 36 MMEB tasks (both in- and out-of-domain) and large relative gains on SCaR.

Reasonably extensive ablations (VLM backbone, instruction presence, image resolution, SAM2 model size, number of MLP layers, segmentation embedding length, LoRA rank, batch size, sampling points) and additional analyses (catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning on SCaR-train, qualitative case studies for on-the-fly correction and in-the-wild I2I retrieval).
Clear writing of the method pipeline and reasonably thorough appendix with dataset details, prompt templates, and reproducibility statement (code/models promised for release).
weaknesses: Fairness-of-comparison concerns: VIRTUE adds an entire pretrained SAM2 segmentation backbone plus a trainable connector on top of the same VLM backbone used by baselines, meaning it has substantially more active parameters/compute at both training and inference time; the paper never reports or controls for this added capacity/latency when claiming state-of-the-art gains at matched '2B'/'7B' model sizes.

The ablation showing that even naive 'Cropped' or 'Prompter' visual-prompt variants recover most of the benefit (e.g., Table 6: Cropped 63.3/25.9 vs Segmentation 64.8/30.4 on MMEB/SCaR) suggests a non-trivial portion of the gain may come from simply having an additional visual-prompt-conditioned stream rather than from the specific entity-level segmentation representations, which is not sufficiently disentangled or discussed.

Benchmark construction and verification both rely on GPT-4V (generation of negatives/missing fields and LLM-based filtering), raising concerns about circularity/self-consistency bias in what passes verification, and about reproducibility given the benchmark depends on a closed, evolving proprietary model; human inspection appears limited to the evaluation split (and only indirectly assessed for the training split via downstream model performance).

The paper's primary motivating scenario in Fig. 1 includes both visual-interactive image-to-image (I2I) and image-to-text (I2T) retrieval, but only I2T (SCaR) is evaluated quantitatively at scale; the I2I setting that opens the paper is relegated to a small, qualitative, non-benchmarked case study in the appendix (E.4.1), making the central claims about visual-interactive capability only partially substantiated.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architectural idea is to prepend an off-the-shelf SAM2 feature map (compressed via Conv2D + MLPs) to the existing VLM-embedder token sequence and train with LoRA/contrastive loss on top of an existing embedding framework (VLM2Vec-style); this is largely engineering integration rather than a new representation-learning or training principle.

The uniform-point-sampling surrogate for non-visual-interactive scenarios is not well motivated theoretically, and the ablation shows no consistent benefit from varying the number of points, raising the question of what aspect of the segmentation-derived tokens is actually contributing to the reported gains versus just adding extra capacity/regularization.

Results are demonstrated only on Qwen2-VL-2B/7B backbones with one segmentation model (SAM2); generality to other VLM architectures or alternative segmentation/visual-prompt encoders is not explored, limiting confidence that the approach generalizes as a 'universal' framework.

Some reported gains in MMEB sub-tasks (e.g., classification, VQA) are modest and the aggregate 'significant improvement' framing in the abstract (3.1%-8.5%) is not consistently reflected at the per-task level, and the paper does not report statistical significance or variance across runs.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: VIRTUE integrates a segmentation model (SAM2) with a VLM-based embedder to support visual-interactive prompts (boxes/points/masks) for representation learning, addressing a genuine gap since current embedding models only accept textual instructions.

New large-scale benchmark (SCaR, ~1M samples across 5 diverse datasets) for visual-interactive image-to-text retrieval, built with a careful multi-stage pipeline (GPT-4V generation of structured object/relation/scene captions and hard negatives via element-swapping, followed by LLM-based verification and human inspection).

Strong and consistent empirical gains: VIRTUE outperforms a wide range of CLIP- and VLM-based baselines on MMEB (3.1%-8.5% improvement) and on SCaR (15.2%-20.3%), across both in-domain and out-of-domain settings and across model sizes (2B/7B).

Extensive and informative ablations/analyses: effect of VLM backbone, instructions, resolution, segmentation streamline alternatives (Prompter, cropping), SAM2 size, MLP depth, segmentation embedding length, LoRA rank, batch size, and sampling points, as well as a catastrophic-forgetting analysis showing VIRTUE is more robust than baselines when fine-tuned on SCaR-train.

Good qualitative/case studies (on-the-fly visual hinting for correction, in-the-wild interactive I2I retrieval) that illustrate practical utility and interpretability of the approach beyond raw metrics.
Paper is clearly written, well-organized, with thorough appendices documenting dataset construction prompts, statistics, and implementation details, aiding reproducibility understanding.
weaknesses: SCaR's ground-truth and negative captions are generated and verified largely by GPT-4V itself (generation + a GPT-4V-based filtering step), which risks circularity and inherited biases/hallucinations in the benchmark despite the added human-inspection step on the evaluation split only (training split quality is only assessed indirectly).

Although the motivating examples (Fig. 1) emphasize both interactive image-to-image and image-to-text retrieval, the paper's main quantitative benchmark (SCaR) and most experiments only cover interactive I2T retrieval; interactive I2I retrieval is relegated to a small, qualitative case study (Appendix E.4.1) without a proper benchmark or quantitative evaluation, which weakens the claimed scope of 'visual-interactive' capability.

Baselines that do not natively support visual prompts are adapted via textualized bounding boxes or naive cropping, which may underestimate what stronger region-aware methods (e.g., grounding-capable VLMs such as Grounding DINO, Ferret, Osprey, mentioned only in related work) could achieve if adapted as embedders; the comparison set, while broad, may not represent the strongest possible baselines for this specific task.

No analysis of the additional computational/latency overhead introduced by incorporating a full SAM2 segmentation model (image encoder, prompt encoder, mask decoder) into the embedding pipeline, which is relevant for practical deployment of an 'embedding model'.
Scalability beyond 7B parameters and generality to other VLM backbones besides Qwen2-VL is not explored, leaving open whether gains persist at larger scales or with different base models.
Some ablation results (e.g., non-monotonic effect of segmentation embedding length |S|, SAM2-L underperforming SAM2-B+ on SCaR) are reported without deeper explanation of why these trends occur.
No variance/statistical significance analysis is reported for the reported improvements across many tasks, making it harder to judge whether all individual gains are robust versus noise.
Full benchmark, model weights, and code are not yet publicly available at submission time (to be released later), which currently limits independent verification of the claims.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: enabling visual-interactive prompts (bbox/point/mask) in VLM-based universal embedding models, which is a meaningful gap relative to existing text-only-instruction embedders.

Introduces a large-scale (1M sample) SCaR benchmark with a carefully designed multi-stage collection pipeline (GPT-4V generation of missing caption elements and hard negatives via object/relation/scene swaps, followed by LLM-based verification with WordNet synonym checks and human inspection with reported inter-annotator agreement).

Extensive empirical evaluation: results on 36 MMEB tasks (IND/OOD) plus 5 SCaR datasets, with consistent and fairly large improvements over numerous CLIP- and VLM-based baselines at both 2B and 7B scale.

Thorough ablation and analysis suite (VLM backbone, instruction presence, resolution, segmentation streamline alternatives, SAM2 size, connector design, embedding length, freezing vs finetuning SAM2, LoRA rank, batch size, robustness to noisy/misaligned prompts, points vs random boxes, latency/memory trade-offs) that substantiates design choices.

Demonstrates that the approach mitigates catastrophic forgetting relative to other baselines when further finetuned on SCaR-train, and shows practical case studies (on-the-fly correction, I2I interactive retrieval) illustrating real-world applicability.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an engineering integration of existing off-the-shelf components (frozen SAM2 + pretrained VLM + LoRA + a conv-MLP connector) rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea, which limits methodological novelty.

SCaR training set quality is only validated indirectly (by training and evaluating downstream performance) rather than through direct human inspection, unlike the more rigorously vetted evaluation set, raising concerns about noise/label quality in the larger training partition.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4V for caption/negative generation raises concerns about inherited biases, potential hallucinated or ambiguous content despite filtering, and reproducibility/cost given the benchmark's dependence on a closed proprietary model.

Baseline comparisons on SCaR textualize bounding boxes for models lacking native visual-prompt support, which is a reasonable but somewhat uneven comparison setup that could understate baseline potential (e.g., with more tailored prompting) and slightly favor the proposed method's design.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (e.g., across seeds) is provided for the performance gains, despite some improvements being relatively modest (e.g., 0.6-1.5 points in several 7B settings).

Interactive image-to-image retrieval, a key motivating use case, is only demonstrated via small-scale qualitative case studies rather than a rigorous quantitative benchmark, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: equipping VLM-based universal embedders with native visual-prompt (point/box/mask) interaction rather than relying solely on text instructions.

Introduces a large (1M-sample) SCaR benchmark spanning five public grounding/captioning datasets, with a reasonably careful construction pipeline combining GPT-4V generation, WordNet-based synonym filtering, and human inspection with reported inter-annotator agreement.

Extensive empirical analysis: ablations over VLM backbone, resolution, segmentation model size/choice, connector design, MLP depth, embedding length, LoRA rank, batch size, as well as robustness tests to noisy/misaligned prompts and random-box sanity checks that support the claim that the model actually uses the visual prompts.

Consistent, reproducible gains over multiple strong, well-chosen baselines (GME, LamRA, VLM2Vec, MMRet, UniME) across both MMEB (36 tasks) and SCaR, with detailed per-task tables and latency/memory analysis.
Good engineering details and reproducibility documentation (training configs, GPU hours, hyperparameters) for both MMEB and SCaR training stages.
weaknesses: The core SCaR benchmark's ground-truth captions and especially its negative candidates are synthetically generated and filtered by GPT-4V itself; only the evaluation split receives full human review while the training split's quality is validated only indirectly (via downstream performance), raising concerns about systematic artifacts/lexical biases that models (including VIRTUE) could exploit rather than genuine compositional reasoning.

Comparisons on SCaR are arguably unfair to baselines: competitor VLMs are only given a textualized bounding-box string appended to the prompt, a format they were never trained to interpret spatially, whereas VIRTUE has a dedicated, purpose-built segmentation branch; this makes it hard to disentangle gains due to "visual interaction" ability versus simply added model capacity/parameters from the SAM2 branch.

On the main MMEB benchmark the improvements over the strongest existing 7B baseline (UniME-7B) are modest (~2 points overall), and the architecture is essentially an engineering combination of an off-the-shelf frozen SAM2 and a VLM rather than a fundamentally new modeling contribution; the segmentation-language connector design space (ablated) shows relatively small differences across variants, suggesting limited sensitivity/insight into why the approach works.

Heavy reliance on a closed, versioned API (GPT-4V) for benchmark construction raises reproducibility concerns, since exact regeneration of SCaR (or extensions to it) may not be possible as the API evolves or is deprecated.

The uniform-sampled-points surrogate for non-interactive scenarios is a somewhat ad hoc design choice (N=9 empirically chosen) without strong theoretical motivation, and its ablation (Fig. 9, Table 5) shows large performance swings that are not deeply analyzed.

Qualitative examples and case studies (Figs. 10–12) are illustrative but anecdotal/small-scale and do not substitute for a rigorous, large-scale human evaluation of SCaR negative quality or in-the-wild I2I retrieval correctness.

The paper's narrative sometimes overstates universality/novelty (e.g., "remains unexplored" applications) while the underlying technique (SAM2 features + frozen VLM + LoRA) is largely a recombination of existing well-known components.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly identified and underexplored gap—visual-interactive capabilities for embedding models—and proposes a reasonably well-motivated architecture (SAM2 + VLM with a segmentation-language connector) to address it.

Extensive experimental validation: results on 36 MMEB tasks (both IND and OOD) and the newly introduced SCaR benchmark, with consistent gains over strong recent baselines (GME, LamRA, VLM2Vec, MMRet, UniME) across both 2B and 7B model scales.

The SCaR benchmark construction is carefully engineered, with a multi-stage LLM-then-human filtering pipeline, WordNet-based synonym checks, inter-annotator agreement reporting (Îş=0.89), and diverse negative generation strategies (scene/relation/object swaps), producing a large-scale (1M sample) and reasonably rigorous resource.

Thorough ablation and robustness studies (segmentation model size, connector design, MLP depth, embedding length, LoRA rank, batch size, robustness to jittered/partial/misaligned prompts, points vs. random boxes) that support the design choices and demonstrate the model genuinely leverages visual prompts rather than ignoring them.

Practical analyses beyond raw accuracy, including catastrophic forgetting comparisons after SCaR fine-tuning, latency/memory trade-offs, and qualitative/in-the-wild case studies (I2I retrieval, on-the-fly VQA correction) that illustrate real-world applicability.

Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations (e.g., no I2I SCaR benchmark due to ethical/copyright concerns, compute constraints limiting training data diversity) and an ethics statement addressing the use of GPT-4V-generated data.
weaknesses: The architectural contribution is largely a combination of existing off-the-shelf components (SAM2, Qwen2-VL) with a connector module; the core novelty is somewhat incremental engineering rather than a fundamentally new learning paradigm.

SCaR benchmark quality depends heavily on GPT-4V for both generation and verification (negatives, missing-element completion, and LLM-based filtering), which risks circularity and inherited biases; the training set quality is only indirectly validated via downstream performance rather than direct human inspection.

Performance gains shrink substantially at larger scale (7B gives only +2.0 on MMEB and +1.5 on SCaR without SCaR-train, vs. +5.1/+6.3 for 2B), raising questions about how the approach scales and whether the entity-level segmentation signal becomes less necessary as base VLM capacity grows.

SCaR evaluates only visual-interactive image-to-text retrieval; image-to-image interactive retrieval is relegated to small-scale, non-standardized case studies (6 images) rather than a proper benchmark, limiting the breadth of claims about "visual-interactive" capability.

A potentially relevant baseline (CLOC/Prompter-based visual grounding) could not be directly compared due to unavailability, leaving the ablation substitute (randomly initialized Transformer) as a weaker proxy comparison.

The textualized-bbox baseline comparisons for non-visually-prompted models may not fully represent the best possible baseline adaptation (e.g., more sophisticated prompting or visual-hint strategies beyond red circles/cropping), potentially overstating the margin of improvement.

Uniform-point sampling as a surrogate for "no visual prompt" scenarios is a somewhat ad hoc design choice whose necessity/optimality is only partially justified (Appendix shows non-monotonic effects of point count).
